t: Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Subarrays With Sum Equals Target — Greedy Prefix Sums
o: We must pick as many disjoint subarrays as possible, each summing exactly to `target`. In Example 1, `[1,1]` twice gives answer 2. In Example 2, three subarrays sum to 6 but they overlap, so the best disjoint selection is 2. Constraints (n up to 1e5) rule out checking all O(n^2) subarrays naively; we need a linear scan. The key structural fact: an exchange argument shows that if any optimal selection exists, one exists where each chosen subarray ends at the earliest possible position — so a greedy left-to-right scan is safe.
k: Greedy works: taking the earliest-ending valid subarray never hurts, since it leaves maximal room for future picks.
Prefix sums + hash map let us detect 'sum equals target' ending at index i in O(1): prefix[i] - target must have appeared before.
After taking a subarray, reset the seen-prefix map to only {0: current} to enforce non-overlap.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force with Greedy Reset
a.i: For each start index, extend rightward accumulating a running sum; when it hits target, count one subarray and jump past its end (greedy). This is O(n^2) worst case but simple and correct.
s: From start, accumulate running sum over j.
When running sum == target, increment count and set start = j+1 (greedy take earliest).
a.t: O(n^2) worst case — for each greedy segment we may scan to the end.

a.n: Approach 2: Prefix Sum Hash Map with Greedy Reset (Optimal)
a.i: Track prefix sums in a hash set/map. At index i, a subarray ending here sums to target iff prefix(i) - target was seen earlier. When found, greedily take it and clear the map (keeping only prefix 0), which guarantees non-overlap and preserves optimality by an exchange argument.
s: If prefix - target is in seen, increment count, reset seen = {0}, prefix = 0.
a.t: O(n) expected — single pass with O(1) average hash operations.
a.sp: O(n) for the hash set of prefix sums within the current segment.

w: Use Approach 2 in interviews: state the greedy exchange argument first (taking the earliest-ending match can't reduce future options), then implement with prefix sums. Pitfalls: negative numbers mean you cannot use sliding window or early termination on sum > target; use 64-bit sums in C++/Java since prefix magnitudes reach ~1e9; remember to reseed the set with 0 after each greedy take. Edge cases: target = 0 (works fine — zero-sum subarrays are counted greedily), all-negative arrays, single element equal to target. Follow-ups: what if subarrays could overlap (then just count all via standard prefix-map counting); what if you wanted minimum-length subarrays instead of maximum count.
